reviewMethod.methodNotesMd: Reviewed the resource-review contract, assessment rubric, fresh-review framework, MolecularSequence context, full StructureDefinition report, direct HTTP/search behavior findings, shared Resource/DomainResource behavior context, deterministic aggregate after forming the resource-level judgment, and the supplied R4/R6 package evidence for resource/search-surface presence. Shared Resource/DomainResource behavior was treated as context only because the assigned artifact is MolecularSequence.

r4Maturity.effectMd: R4 MolecularSequence was trial-use/FMM 1, so the compatibility burden is materially weaker than for mature or normative resources. That makes removal of an immature genomics model more plausible, but it does not erase the safety and interoperability concern around migrating sequence coordinates, allele facts, quality data, repositories, and clinical genomics reporting patterns.

overall.oneLineConclusion: MolecularSequence has a resource-identity removal in R6 core, so a resource-level migration program is unavoidable; standards effort should focus on the removal/mapping decision rather than preserving isolated local paths.

reasoning.thesisMd: MolecularSequence is not a mostly-stable resource with a few local breaks. The R4 resource type and its R4-specific search surface exist in the supplied R4 package, while the supplied R6 core package has no same-name resource or MolecularSequence search parameters. A conformant R4 `resourceType: "MolecularSequence"` instance therefore cannot become R6-core-conformant by element renaming or cardinality adjustment; implementers need an R4 compatibility island, a non-core/IG replacement, or a domain-specific mapping into other R6 resources/profiles.
reasoning.migrationShapeMd: The migration shape is resource removal/replacement plus loss of a specialized local model. R4 MolecularSequence includes required coordinate-system data and local content for reference sequences, variants, observed sequence, quality metrics, repositories, pointers, and structural variants. The available R6 core package does not provide a computable successor for those fields, so migration requires genomics policy choices and tests for coordinate conventions, allele/reference identity, quality interpretation, repository access, and structural-variant boundaries.
reasoning.compatibilityLeverageMd: Because the resource identity is gone, a migration program dominates: preserving one more local element name or terminology binding inside the removed base resource would not by itself make R4 instances valid in R6. That does lower the leverage of isolated endpoint, search-parameter, or terminology preservation once the removal is accepted. It does not mean compatibility is worthless: the high-value compatibility question is whether R6 should retain a deprecated/retired MolecularSequence transition surface or publish an official computable migration artifact so historical genomic data can be validated and transformed safely.
reasoning.lessBreakingAlternativesMd: The most meaningful less-breaking alternative is at the resource/transition level, not at individual child elements: keep MolecularSequence as deprecated or retired for one transition release, or provide a named successor/profile plus ConceptMap/StructureMap covering sequence type, coordinate system, reference sequence alternatives, variants, quality, repository, and structural variant details. Carrying the full low-FMM model forward has real cost and could prolong duplicate genomics representations, but publishing a computable bridge is lower risk than leaving every implementer to infer the replacement.
reasoning.behaviorImpactMd: The direct HTTP and SearchParameter findings are real for MolecularSequence: base CapabilityStatement endpoint advertisements and R4 MolecularSequence-only search parameters disappear with the removed resource. They are best understood as derivative API consequences of the resource-identity decision, not independent reasons to score another major migration. Shared Resource/DomainResource operation/search changes may affect generic infrastructure, but they were not counted as MolecularSequence-specific because MolecularSequence is not Resource or DomainResource.
reasoning.comparisonToDeterministicAggregateMd: The deterministic aggregate also concluded `Yes`, `removed-or-replaced-resource`, and `migration-program-dominates`. I agree with that headline because the resource identity is absent from R6 core. The nuance is that migration dominance should not be read as approval of the removal without transition support: the identity-removal and no-computable-successor findings remain standards-review-worthy, while terminology and grouped REST/search losses are mostly local consequences once the broader resource removal is accepted.
reasoning.uncertaintyMd: Confidence is high that the supplied R6 core package lacks MolecularSequence and its same-name search parameters. Confidence is lower on the intended replacement because the local inputs did not include official ballot rationale, Clinical Genomics companion packages, or a cross-version ConceptMap/StructureMap.

findingConsiderations.title: MolecularSequence resource is present in R4 but absent from the R6 core package
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This is the decisive break. Old R4 instances fail before child-element validation because R6 core has no MolecularSequence StructureDefinition, parser registry target, resource endpoint, or conformance identity. Even with FMM 1, complete resource identity removal is the reason a resource-level migration program is unavoidable.

findingConsiderations.title: R4 MolecularSequence local content model has no computable R6 core successor
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This shows that migration is not merely changing `resourceType`. The R4 sequence, coordinate, allele, quality, repository, pointer, and structural-variant content needs domain-specific mapping, making a computable migration guide or successor profile safety-relevant even though the source resource is low maturity.

findingConsiderations.title: R6 generated models, parsers, and REST/search APIs will not expose MolecularSequence
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This is an important implementation consequence: generated R6 libraries and route/search registries will drop MolecularSequence. It matters for migration planning and compatibility adapters, but it does not independently change the resource-level conclusion because it follows directly from the resource removal.

findingConsiderations.title: MolecularSequence-specific R4 terminology artifacts are absent from the R6 core package
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: Preserving retired terminology could help mixed-version validators, but the absence of these terminology artifacts is mostly a local migration chore once the base resource and bound elements are removed. Historical R4 validation can still load the R4 package; R6 migration should explicitly map or carry the old code systems where needed.

findingConsiderations.title: The full base CapabilityStatement no longer advertises many R4 resource REST endpoints
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: MolecularSequence is one of the removed advertised endpoints. This affects generic clients and conformance tooling, but for this resource it is derivative of the same resource-identity removal; preserving endpoint aliases would effectively require retaining a legacy MolecularSequence surface.

findingConsiderations.title: Search parameters whose only R4 bases were removed resources disappear from the R6 search surface
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: The R4 MolecularSequence search parameters disappear because the R6 endpoint/base is gone. This is high-risk for clients that used patient, type, chromosome, variant-coordinate, or window-coordinate searches, but the right fix depends on the resource migration target rather than preserving search metadata in isolation.

findingConsiderations.title: Required input parameter renamed from `input` to `resource`
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This is a shared Resource operation behavior change and may affect generic conversion workflows, including those used during MolecularSequence migration. It was not counted as MolecularSequence-specific because the assigned artifact is not Resource or DomainResource.

findingConsiderations.title: Core special/profile search parameters changed type metadata for _content, _text, _query, and _profile
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This shared search metadata change can affect generic infrastructure, but it does not alter the MolecularSequence resource-level judgment. The MolecularSequence-specific search break is the loss of resource-base search parameters after resource removal.

recommendedNextActions.actionMd: Standards review should explicitly document the intended R6 replacement or retirement path for MolecularSequence, including whether a deprecated/retired transition StructureDefinition is warranted despite the R4 FMM 1 status.

Publish or require a computable migration artifact for clinically relevant MolecularSequence content: coordinate system, reference sequence identity, observed/reference alleles, quality metrics, repository pointers, and structural variant boundaries.

Treat MolecularSequence REST endpoints and search parameters as migration surfaces tied to the chosen replacement. If no R6 core endpoint is retained, document legacy adapter expectations and query mappings rather than leaving clients to infer them from missing metadata.

For systems carrying historical MolecularSequence data forward, preserve R4 terminology package access or define explicit code maps for sequence type, orientation, strand, quality, repository type, chromosome/reference sequence, and structural variant type.

caveats: Only the supplied R4/R6 core packages and local reports were reviewed; non-core Clinical Genomics implementation guides or companion ballot packages may define the intended R6 replacement.
No official R4-to-R6 ballot rationale, deprecation note, ConceptMap, or StructureMap was present in the local inputs.
R4 MolecularSequence is FMM 1/trial-use, so prevalence and stability expectations should be treated as lower than for mature clinical resources even though the data domain can be safety-sensitive.
The direct behavior findings are grouped findings across many removed resources; this review only uses their MolecularSequence-specific implications.
